claim: Friedreich's ataxia (FRDA) is an autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disease caused by mutations in Frataxin (FXN).
source: Friedreich's ataxia (FRDA) is an autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disease caused by mutations in Frataxin (FXN).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about FRDA and is stated as a fact in the abstract.

claim: Loss of FXN causes impaired mitochondrial function and iron homeostasis.
source: Loss of FXN causes impaired mitochondrial function and iron homeostasis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about FXN function, stated as fact in the abstract.

claim: An elevated production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) was previously proposed to contribute to the pathogenesis of FRDA.
source: An elevated production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) was previously proposed to contribute to the pathogenesis of FRDA.
evidence: This refers to previous proposals in the literature about ROS in FRDA pathogenesis.

claim: Loss of frataxin homolog (fh), a Drosophila homolog of FXN, causes a ROS independent neurodegeneration in flies.
source: We recently showed that loss of frataxin homolog (fh), a Drosophila homolog of FXN, causes a ROS independent neurodegeneration in flies (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2016, which is the authors' previous work.

claim: In fh mutants, iron accumulation in the nervous system enhances the synthesis of sphingolipids.
source: In fh mutants, iron accumulation in the nervous system enhances the synthesis of sphingolipids, which in turn activates 3-phosphoinositide dependent protein kinase-1 (Pdk1) and myocyte enhancer factor-2 (Mef2) to trigger neurodegeneration of adult photoreceptors.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2016 in the previous sentence.

claim: In fh mutants, sphingolipids activate 3-phosphoinositide dependent protein kinase-1 (Pdk1) and myocyte enhancer factor-2 (Mef2) to trigger neurodegeneration of adult photoreceptors.
source: In fh mutants, iron accumulation in the nervous system enhances the synthesis of sphingolipids, which in turn activates 3-phosphoinositide dependent protein kinase-1 (Pdk1) and myocyte enhancer factor-2 (Mef2) to trigger neurodegeneration of adult photoreceptors.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2016 in the previous sentence.

claim: Loss of Fxn in the nervous system in mice activates an iron/sphingolipid/PDK1/Mef2 pathway.
source: Here, we show that loss of Fxn in the nervous system in mice also activates an iron/sphingolipid/PDK1/Mef2 pathway, indicating that the mechanism is evolutionarily conserved.
evidence: This is the main finding of the current study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The iron/sphingolipid/PDK1/Mef2 pathway mechanism is evolutionarily conserved.
source: Here, we show that loss of Fxn in the nervous system in mice also activates an iron/sphingolipid/PDK1/Mef2 pathway, indicating that the mechanism is evolutionarily conserved.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the pathway is activated in both flies and mice.

claim: Sphingolipid levels are increased in hearts of FRDA patients.
source: Furthermore, sphingolipid levels and PDK1 activity are also increased in hearts of FRDA patients, suggesting that a similar pathway is affected in FRDA.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: PDK1 activity is increased in hearts of FRDA patients.
source: Furthermore, sphingolipid levels and PDK1 activity are also increased in hearts of FRDA patients, suggesting that a similar pathway is affected in FRDA.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A similar pathway is affected in FRDA.
source: Furthermore, sphingolipid levels and PDK1 activity are also increased in hearts of FRDA patients, suggesting that a similar pathway is affected in FRDA.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of increased sphingolipids and PDK1 activity in FRDA patient hearts.

claim: FRDA is the most prevalent form of recessive cerebellar ataxia characterized by neurodegeneration and cardiomyopathy.
source: FRDA is the most prevalent form of recessive cerebellar ataxia characterized by neurodegeneration and cardiomyopathy.
evidence: This is established knowledge about FRDA.

claim: Patients with FRDA exhibit a progressive degeneration of the dorsal root ganglia, sensory peripheral nerves, and dentate nuclei of the cerebellum.
source: Patients with FRDA exhibit a progressive degeneration of the dorsal root ganglia, sensory peripheral nerves, and dentate nuclei of the cerebellum.
evidence: This is established knowledge about FRDA pathology.

claim: Most individuals with FRDA develop several neurological symptoms at a juvenile age.
source: Most individuals develop several neurological symptoms at a juvenile age, but individuals with adult or late onset are occasionally reported (Koeppen, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Koeppen, 2011.

claim: Individuals with adult or late onset FRDA are occasionally reported.
source: Most individuals develop several neurological symptoms at a juvenile age, but individuals with adult or late onset are occasionally reported (Koeppen, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Koeppen, 2011.

claim: Mutations in FXN were discovered as the primary cause of FRDA.
source: Mutations in FXN were discovered as the primary cause of FRDA (Campuzano et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Campuzano et al., 1996.

claim: Studies of the yeast frataxin homolog identified a role for FXN in iron-sulfur cluster biosynthesis and iron homeostasis.
source: Studies of the yeast frataxin homolog identified a role for FXN in iron-sulfur cluster biosynthesis and iron homeostasis (Babcock et al., 1997; Mühlenhoff et al., 2002; Rötig et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Babcock et al., 1997; Mühlenhoff et al., 2002; Rötig et al., 1997.

claim: Loss of FXN has been shown to cause mitochondrial dysfunction in several model organisms.
source: Loss of FXN has been shown to cause mitochondrial dysfunction in several model organisms (Anderson et al., 2005; Puccio et al., 2001; Rötig et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Anderson et al., 2005; Puccio et al., 2001; Rötig et al., 1997.

claim: Whether iron accumulates in the nervous system is still under debate.
source: Yet, whether iron accumulates in the nervous system is still under debate, as it has been reported that iron levels are not altered in the nervous system of a conditional knockout mouse model and in FRDA patients (Puccio et al., 2001; Simon et al., 2004; Solbach et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Puccio et al., 2001; Simon et al., 2004; Solbach et al., 2014.

claim: Iron levels are not altered in the nervous system of a conditional knockout mouse model and in FRDA patients.
source: Yet, whether iron accumulates in the nervous system is still under debate, as it has been reported that iron levels are not altered in the nervous system of a conditional knockout mouse model and in FRDA patients (Puccio et al., 2001; Simon et al., 2004; Solbach et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Puccio et al., 2001; Simon et al., 2004; Solbach et al., 2014.

claim: In FRDA patients, iron was shown to accumulate in the dentate nuclei or in glia cells of dorsal root ganglia.
source: However, in FRDA patients, iron was shown to accumulate in the dentate nuclei or in glia cells of dorsal root ganglia (Boddaert et al., 2007; Koeppen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boddaert et al., 2007; Koeppen et al., 2009.

claim: The iron deposition phenotype is still controversial in mouse models and FRDA patients.
source: In sum, the iron deposition phenotype is still controversial in mouse models and FRDA patients, and the role of iron in the pathophysiology of FRDA has not yet been determined.
evidence: This is inferred from the conflicting reports cited in the previous sentences.

claim: The role of iron in the pathophysiology of FRDA has not yet been determined.
source: In sum, the iron deposition phenotype is still controversial in mouse models and FRDA patients, and the role of iron in the pathophysiology of FRDA has not yet been determined.
evidence: This is inferred from the conflicting reports and lack of consensus in the literature.

claim: It has been proposed that ROS, generated by impaired mitochondrial electron transport chain complexes or iron deposition, mediate the pathogenesis in FRDA.
source: It has been proposed that ROS, generated by impaired mitochondrial electron transport chain complexes or iron deposition, mediate the pathogenesis in FRDA (Bayot et al., 2011; Santos et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bayot et al., 2011; Santos et al., 2010.

claim: Emerging evidence suggests that ROS are not elevated in several model organisms.
source: However, emerging evidence suggests that ROS are not elevated in several model organisms, and several clinical trials based on antioxidant therapy have shown no or limited benefit in FRDA patients (Babcock et al., 1997; Llorens et al., 2007; Macevilly and Muller, 1997; Santhera Pharmaceuticals, 2010; Seznec et al., 2005; Shidara and Hollenbeck, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Babcock et al., 1997; Llorens et al., 2007; Macevilly and Muller, 1997; Santhera Pharmaceuticals, 2010; Seznec et al., 2005; Shidara and Hollenbeck, 2010.

claim: Several clinical trials based on antioxidant therapy have shown no or limited benefit in FRDA patients.
source: However, emerging evidence suggests that ROS are not elevated in several model organisms, and several clinical trials based on antioxidant therapy have shown no or limited benefit in FRDA patients (Babcock et al., 1997; Llorens et al., 2007; Macevilly and Muller, 1997; Santhera Pharmaceuticals, 2010; Seznec et al., 2005; Shidara and Hollenbeck, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Babcock et al., 1997; Llorens et al., 2007; Macevilly and Muller, 1997; Santhera Pharmaceuticals, 2010; Seznec et al., 2005; Shidara and Hollenbeck, 2010.

claim: The pathogenesis of FRDA is still poorly understood.
source: Hence, the pathogenesis of this disease is still poorly understood.
evidence: This is inferred from the conflicting evidence and failed clinical trials discussed in the previous paragraphs.

claim: Loss of fh in Drosophila leads to iron accumulation in the nervous system.
source: We showed that loss of fh in Drosophila leads to iron accumulation in the nervous system, which in turn induces sphingolipid synthesis and ectopically activates Pdk1 and Mef2.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2016 in the previous sentence.

claim: Iron accumulation in Drosophila fh mutants induces sphingolipid synthesis and ectopically activates Pdk1 and Mef2.
source: We showed that loss of fh in Drosophila leads to iron accumulation in the nervous system, which in turn induces sphingolipid synthesis and ectopically activates Pdk1 and Mef2.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2016 in the previous sentence.

claim: Mef2 activation triggers the aberrant transcription of downstream target genes that causes the degeneration of fly photoreceptors.
source: Mef2 activation triggers the aberrant transcription of downstream target genes that causes the degeneration of fly photoreceptors (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2016.

claim: The Fxn-sgRNAs induce lesions in the Fxn locus and reduce the levels of FXN protein when compared to the LacZ-sgRNA control in Neuro-2a cells.
source: The Fxn-sgRNAs induce lesions in the Fxn locus and reduce the levels of FXN protein when compared to the LacZ-sgRNA control in Neuro-2a cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The majority of cortical neurons are infected with AAV.
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, the majority of cortical neurons are infected with AAV, and the mRNA levels of Fxn in Fxn-sgRNA mice are less than 40% of the LacZ-sgRNA control mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The mRNA levels of Fxn in Fxn-sgRNA mice are less than 40% of the LacZ-sgRNA control mice.
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, the majority of cortical neurons are infected with AAV, and the mRNA levels of Fxn in Fxn-sgRNA mice are less than 40% of the LacZ-sgRNA control mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: At approximately four months of age the Fxn-sgRNA mice develop an abnormal appearance when compared to LacZ-sgRNA control mice.
source: At approximately four months of age the Fxn-sgRNA mice (mice with Fxn-sgRNA AAV injection) develop an abnormal appearance when compared to LacZ-sgRNA control mice.
evidence: This is supported by observations described in the manuscript.

claim: Fxn-sgRNA mice have a smaller body size and a hunchback phenotype at P130.
source: These include a smaller body size and a hunchback phenotype at P130 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The features of Fxn-sgRNA mice are similar to the neuronal conditional knockout mice that were previously reported.
source: Interestingly, these features are similar to the neuronal conditional knockout mice that were previously reported (Puccio et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Puccio et al., 2001.

claim: The Fxn-sgRNA mice become much less mobile than their LacZ-sgRNA littermates.
source: In addition, the Fxn-sgRNA mice become much less mobile than their LacZ-sgRNA littermates (Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Videos 1 and 2.

claim: The Fxn-sgRNA mice display an aberrant reflex when lifted by the tail as they fail to spread their hind limbs.
source: The Fxn-sgRNA mice also display an aberrant reflex when lifted by the tail as they fail to spread their hind limbs (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: At P50, there is no difference between LacZ-sgRNA and Fxn-sgRNA mice in the rotarod test.
source: At P50, we observe no difference between LacZ-sgRNA and Fxn-sgRNA mice.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Fxn-sgRNA mice show a significant reduction of latency to fall from the rod at age of P130.
source: However, Fxn-sgRNA mice show a significant reduction of latency to fall from the rod at age of P130 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Fxn-sgRNA mice show a severe impairment in the wire hang test at P130.
source: Besides the deficit on the rotarod test, Fxn-sgRNA mice also show a severe impairment in the wire hang test at P130 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: A removal of Fxn in a substantial neuronal population in the newborn mouse brain causes a severe impairment of neuronal function.
source: In summary, a removal of Fxn in a substantial neuronal population in the newborn mouse brain causes a severe impairment of neuronal function.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral and motor deficits observed in Fxn-sgRNA mice.

claim: ATF3 is up-regulated in cortical neurons of Fxn-sgRNA mice.
source: We observed that the activating transcription factor 3 (ATF3), a marker that is typically associated with cellular stress response and neuronal damage (Tsujino et al., 2000), is up-regulated in cortical neurons of Fxn-sgRNA mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: ATF3 is a marker that is typically associated with cellular stress response and neuronal damage.
source: We observed that the activating transcription factor 3 (ATF3), a marker that is typically associated with cellular stress response and neuronal damage (Tsujino et al., 2000), is up-regulated in cortical neurons of Fxn-sgRNA mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tsujino et al., 2000.

claim: No ATF3 positive cells were observed in LacZ-sgRNA mice.
source: However, no ATF3 positive cells were observed in LacZ-sgRNA mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The axon initial segments are lost in cortical neurons of Fxn-sgRNA mice.
source: In addition, the axon initial segments, specialized membrane regions where Na+ channels cluster to initiate action potentials (Szu-Yu Ho and Rasband, 2011), are lost in cortical neurons of Fxn-sgRNA mice.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Axon initial segments are specialized membrane regions where Na+ channels cluster to initiate action potentials.
source: In addition, the axon initial segments, specialized membrane regions where Na+ channels cluster to initiate action potentials (Szu-Yu Ho and Rasband, 2011), are lost in cortical neurons of Fxn-sgRNA mice.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Szu-Yu Ho and Rasband, 2011.

claim: AnkG is severely reduced or lost in cortical neurons in Fxn-sgRNA mice, especially in ATF3 positive neurons.
source: As shown in Figure 2B, the scaffolding protein required for the formation and maintenance of the axon initial segment, ankyrin-G (AnkG), is severely reduced or lost in cortical neurons in Fxn-sgRNA mice, especially in ATF3 positive neurons (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: AnkG is a scaffolding protein required for the formation and maintenance of the axon initial segment.
source: As shown in Figure 2B, the scaffolding protein required for the formation and maintenance of the axon initial segment, ankyrin-G (AnkG), is severely reduced or lost in cortical neurons in Fxn-sgRNA mice, especially in ATF3 positive neurons (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about AnkG function.

claim: Loss of Fxn in cortical neurons leads to severe neuronal injury and damage.
source: These data suggest that loss of Fxn in cortical neurons leads to severe neuronal injury and damage.
evidence: This is inferred from the ATF3 upregulation and AnkG loss observed in Fxn-sgRNA mice.

claim: The DAB signal is strongly increased in brain sections of Fxn-sgRNA mice when compared to control mice at P130.
source: At P130 the DAB signal is strongly increased in brain sections of Fxn-sgRNA mice when compared to control mice (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The majority of DAB signals are co-localized with a neuronal marker but not glial markers.
source: Interestingly, the majority of DAB signals are co-localized with a neuronal marker but not glial markers, suggesting that Fe3+ accumulates in neurons, although there are some weak diffuse signals distributed outside of the cell body (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Fe3+ accumulates in neurons upon loss of Fxn.
source: Interestingly, the majority of DAB signals are co-localized with a neuronal marker but not glial markers, suggesting that Fe3+ accumulates in neurons, although there are some weak diffuse signals distributed outside of the cell body (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the co-localization of DAB signals with neuronal markers.

claim: Fe3+ accumulates in the nervous system upon loss of Fxn.
source: These data show that Fe3+ accumulates in the nervous system upon loss of Fxn.
evidence: This is supported by the Perls'/DAB staining data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The use of DAB to enhance the Perls' Prussian blue staining allowed observation of Fe3+ accumulation, whereas previous reports did not observe it.
source: The fact that we observed an obvious Fe3+ accumulation, whereas previous reports did not, is likely due to the use of DAB to enhance the Perls' Prussian blue staining, as we did not observe any signal with Perls' Prussian blue staining alone (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of Perls' staining with and without DAB enhancement.

claim: No signal was observed with Perls' Prussian blue staining alone.
source: The fact that we observed an obvious Fe3+ accumulation, whereas previous reports did not, is likely due to the use of DAB to enhance the Perls' Prussian blue staining, as we did not observe any signal with Perls' Prussian blue staining alone (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: RPA is a cell-permeable fluorescent dye that selectively accumulates in mitochondria.
source: RPA is a cell-permeable fluorescent dye that selectively accumulates in mitochondria, and its fluorescence is stoichiometrically quenched by Fe2+ (Petrat et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Petrat et al., 2002.

claim: RPA fluorescence is stoichiometrically quenched by Fe2+.
source: RPA is a cell-permeable fluorescent dye that selectively accumulates in mitochondria, and its fluorescence is stoichiometrically quenched by Fe2+ (Petrat et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Petrat et al., 2002.

claim: Fe2+ accumulates in the brain of Fxn-sgRNA mice at P60.
source: Interestingly, we observed Fe2+ accumulation in the brain of Fxn-sgRNA mice at P60, a time point at which we did not observe behavioral defects in the Fxn-sgRNA mice.
evidence: This is supported by RPA staining data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: At P60, behavioral defects were not observed in the Fxn-sgRNA mice.
source: Interestingly, we observed Fe2+ accumulation in the brain of Fxn-sgRNA mice at P60, a time point at which we did not observe behavioral defects in the Fxn-sgRNA mice.
evidence: This is supported by the rotarod test data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The RPA fluorescence is quenched in cells of cortical layer IV and V of Fxn-sgRNA mice when compared to LacZ-sgRNA controls.
source: As shown in Figure 3B, the RPA fluorescence is quenched in cells of cortical layer IV and V of Fxn-sgRNA mice when compared to LacZ-sgRNA controls, indicating an accumulation of Fe2+ in the nervous system upon loss of Fxn.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Fe2+ accumulates in the nervous system upon loss of Fxn.
source: As shown in Figure 3B, the RPA fluorescence is quenched in cells of cortical layer IV and V of Fxn-sgRNA mice when compared to LacZ-sgRNA controls, indicating an accumulation of Fe2+ in the nervous system upon loss of Fxn.
evidence: This is inferred from the quenching of RPA fluorescence in Fxn-sgRNA mice.

claim: RPAC is a dye that is structurally very similar to RPA but is insensitive to Fe2+ mediated fluorescence quenching.
source: As a negative control, we used RPAC, a dye that is structurally very similar to RPA but is insensitive to Fe2+ mediated fluorescence quenching.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RPAC properties.

claim: RPAC is present at similar levels in both Fxn-sgRNA and LacZ-sgRNA brains.
source: RPAC is present at similar levels in both Fxn-sgRNA and LacZ-sgRNA brains (Figure 3B), suggesting that the decreased fluorescence of RPA in Fxn-sgRNA mice is not due to impaired dye uptake but due to Fe2+ quenching.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The decreased fluorescence of RPA in Fxn-sgRNA mice is not due to impaired dye uptake but due to Fe2+ quenching.
source: RPAC is present at similar levels in both Fxn-sgRNA and LacZ-sgRNA brains (Figure 3B), suggesting that the decreased fluorescence of RPA in Fxn-sgRNA mice is not due to impaired dye uptake but due to Fe2+ quenching.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar RPAC levels in both groups.

claim: It was previously proposed that iron deposition triggers free radical production via Fenton's reaction.
source: It was previously proposed that iron deposition triggers free radical production via Fenton's reaction.
evidence: This is established knowledge about iron-mediated oxidative stress.

claim: 4-HNE is a major product of lipid peroxidation.
source: We therefore measured oxidative stress by examining the levels of 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE), a major product of lipid peroxidation (Ayala et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ayala et al., 2014.

claim: No increase of 4-HNE was observed in Fxn-sgRNA brain tissues.
source: However, we did not observe an increase of 4-HNE in Fxn-sgRNA brain tissues (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), consistent with previous observations in flies (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The lack of 4-HNE increase in Fxn-sgRNA brain tissues is consistent with previous observations in flies.
source: However, we did not observe an increase of 4-HNE in Fxn-sgRNA brain tissues (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), consistent with previous observations in flies (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2016.

claim: Phosphorylation of S241 in the PDK1 activation loop is required for its activity.
source: Phosphorylation of S241 in the PDK1 activation loop is required for its activity (Casamayor et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Casamayor et al., 1999.

claim: An increase in phosphorylation levels of S241 in PDK1 was observed in Fxn-sgRNA mice compared to the LacZ-sgRNA mice at P60.
source: We observed an increase in phosphorylation levels of S241 in Fxn-sgRNA mice compared to the LacZ-sgRNA mice at P60, prior to the onset of symptoms (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The increase in PDK1 phosphorylation occurs prior to the onset of symptoms.
source: We observed an increase in phosphorylation levels of S241 in Fxn-sgRNA mice compared to the LacZ-sgRNA mice at P60, prior to the onset of symptoms (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that P60 is before the onset of behavioral defects observed at P130.

claim: Many, but not all, Mef2 downstream target transcripts are up-regulated 1.5–3 fold in Fxn-sgRNA mice at P60.
source: As shown in Figure 3D, many, but not all, transcripts are up-regulated 1.5–3 fold in Fxn-sgRNA mice at P60.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Only about half of Mef2 targets are up-regulated (to 2–3 fold) when Mef2A is overexpressed.
source: This is consistent with previous findings that only about half of Mef2 targets are up-regulated (to 2–3 fold) when Mef2A is overexpressed (Ewen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ewen et al., 2011.

claim: The PDK1/Mef2 pathway is activated in the vertebrate nervous system upon loss of Fxn prior to the onset of phenotypes.
source: In summary, these results provide evidence that the PDK1/Mef2 pathway is activated in the vertebrate nervous system upon loss of Fxn prior to the onset of phenotypes that are observed about two months later.
evidence: This is inferred from the PDK1 phosphorylation and Mef2 target upregulation at P60, before behavioral defects at P130.

claim: Heart samples of FRDA patients were previously shown to accumulate Fe3+.
source: As we were unable to obtain cerebella and dorsal root ganglia of patients, we used heart samples that were previously shown to accumulate Fe3+ (Bradley et al., 2000; Koeppen, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bradley et al., 2000; Koeppen, 2011.

claim: A substantial fraction of the sphingolipids are increased in FRDA patients when compared to controls.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, a substantial fraction of the sphingolipids are increased in FRDA patients when compared to controls, including short chain ceramides (C14-C18), different dihydroceramides, dihydrosphingosines, dihydrosphingosine-1-phosphate, and sphingosine.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Short chain ceramides (C14-C18) are increased in FRDA patients when compared to controls.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, a substantial fraction of the sphingolipids are increased in FRDA patients when compared to controls, including short chain ceramides (C14-C18), different dihydroceramides, dihydrosphingosines, dihydrosphingosine-1-phosphate, and sphingosine.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Different dihydroceramides are increased in FRDA patients when compared to controls.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, a substantial fraction of the sphingolipids are increased in FRDA patients when compared to controls, including short chain ceramides (C14-C18), different dihydroceramides, dihydrosphingosines, dihydrosphingosine-1-phosphate, and sphingosine.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Dihydrosphingosines are increased in FRDA patients when compared to controls.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, a substantial fraction of the sphingolipids are increased in FRDA patients when compared to controls, including short chain ceramides (C14-C18), different dihydroceramides, dihydrosphingosines, dihydrosphingosine-1-phosphate, and sphingosine.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Dihydrosphingosine-1-phosphate is increased in FRDA patients when compared to controls.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, a substantial fraction of the sphingolipids are increased in FRDA patients when compared to controls, including short chain ceramides (C14-C18), different dihydroceramides, dihydrosphingosines, dihydrosphingosine-1-phosphate, and sphingosine.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Sphingosine is increased in FRDA patients when compared to controls.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, a substantial fraction of the sphingolipids are increased in FRDA patients when compared to controls, including short chain ceramides (C14-C18), different dihydroceramides, dihydrosphingosines, dihydrosphingosine-1-phosphate, and sphingosine.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The phosphorylation levels of S241 in PDK1 are elevated in FRDA patients when compared to controls.
source: The phosphorylation levels of S241 in PDK1 are elevated in FRDA patients when compared to controls (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Patient six showed no obvious increase in PDK1 phosphorylation when compared to the other patients.
source: Note that patient six showed no obvious increase in PDK1 phosphorylation when compared to the other patients.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Patient six had relatively mild symptoms and a later onset of disease (age 18) than other patients (ages 4 to 9).
source: This patient had relatively mild symptoms and a later onset of disease (age 18) than other patients (ages 4 to 9).
evidence: This is supported by clinical data shown in Table 1.

claim: The age of death was much later in patient 6 (age 67) compared to the other patients (age 25–37).
source: The age of death was also much later in patient 6 (age 67) compared to the other patients (age 25–37).
evidence: This is supported by clinical data shown in Table 1.

claim: The increased levels of sphingolipids in patient six are less pronounced than other patients.
source: Similarly, the increased levels of sphingolipids in patient six are also less pronounced than other patients.
evidence: This is inferred from the sphingolipid profiling data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The iron/sphingolipid/PDK1/Mef2 pathway is activated in FRDA patients.
source: In sum, these data suggest that the iron/sphingolipid/PDK1/Mef2 pathway is activated in FRDA patients and that it may contribute to the pathogenesis of FRDA.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased sphingolipids and PDK1 activity in FRDA patient hearts.

claim: The iron/sphingolipid/PDK1/Mef2 pathway may contribute to the pathogenesis of FRDA.
source: In sum, these data suggest that the iron/sphingolipid/PDK1/Mef2 pathway is activated in FRDA patients and that it may contribute to the pathogenesis of FRDA.

claim: Removal of Fxn in the central nervous system using AAV and CRISPR/Cas9 causes behavioral and neurological phenotypes in mice.
